meaning: Linked to the suffering servant (Isaiah 53) and the annual Torah reading cycle
description: The number 53 is best known for its connection to Isaiah chapter 53, which describes the suffering servant – one of the most debated and central passages in both Jewish and Christian theology. In Jewish tradition, this chapter is interpreted as a description of the people of Israel in suffering and exile, while the Christian tradition sees it as a prophecy about the Messiah's substitutionary suffering. The number also has liturgical significance through the division of the Torah into weekly reading portions (parashot). The Torah has 54 parashot in total, but in a common (non-leap) year some portions are combined so that in practice 53 portions are read through the annual cycle. In this way, the number 53 is linked to the completion of the Torah's annual reading cycle.

versions.meaning: The number 53 has no prominent independent symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.

Beyond these contextual associations, the number 53 does not itself hold a widely recognized independent symbolic value in numerology or gematria within Jewish tradition.

footnotes.text: The number of parashot is formally 54, but in years without extra Sabbaths (non-leap years), some portions are combined, so the actual number of readings throughout the year often becomes 53.

In 2 Chronicles 2:16, the number 53 appears as part of the census of foreign men in Israel under Solomon: 153,600. Although the number here is part of a larger figure, it is one of the rare biblical occurrences where 53 is explicitly mentioned.
The number 53 has no widely recognized independent symbolic value in classical gematria or Jewish numerology beyond its contextual links to Isaiah 53 and the Torah portions.
